questions.question: Inside a bar magnet, the direction of the magnetic field lines is:
options: From the N-pole to the S-pole
From the S-pole to the N-pole
Undefined, because the field inside a magnet is zero
Perpendicular to the axis of the magnet

solution.key_concept: Magnetic field lines are closed loops. They run N to S outside the magnet and S to N inside it.
steps: Outside the magnet, the lines leave the N-pole and enter the S-pole.
Field lines are continuous closed loops, so they must return from S to N inside the magnet.
solution.final_answer: Option (2): From the S-pole to the N-pole
solution.why_not_others: N to S is the direction outside the magnet only. The field inside is not zero, because the lines pass through the magnet. The lines inside run along the axis, not perpendicular to it.
solution.common_trap: Assuming field lines run N to S everywhere, as electric lines run from + to -.
solution.time_saving_tip: Closed loops mean the inside direction must be opposite to the outside direction.

questions.question: A bar magnet has pole strength $5\ \text{A m}$ and magnetic length $10\ \text{cm}$. It is cut into two equal halves by a cut perpendicular to its axis. What are the pole strength and magnetic moment of each piece?

solution.key_concept: A cut perpendicular to the axis keeps the pole strength the same and halves the length, so the moment is halved.
steps: Original moment: $m=q_m(2l)=5\times0.10=0.5\ \text{A m}^2$.
Each piece keeps $q_m=5\ \text{A m}$ and has length $5\ \text{cm}$.
New moment: $m'=5\times0.05=0.25\ \text{A m}^2$.
solution.why_not_others: Halving the pole strength applies to a cut along the axis, not perpendicular to it. Halving both the pole strength and the length would quarter the moment. Keeping the moment at 0.5 ignores the reduced length.
solution.common_trap: Mixing up the effects of an axial cut and a perpendicular cut.

questions.question: A solenoid of 200 turns, each of area $5\ \text{cm}^2$, carries a current of $2\ \text{A}$. It is to be replaced by a bar magnet of equal magnetic moment and magnetic length $4\ \text{cm}$. The pole strength of the magnet must be:

solution.key_concept: A solenoid has moment $NIA$, and an equivalent magnet satisfies $m=q_m(2l)$.
steps: $m=NIA=200\times2\times5\times10^{-4}=0.2\ \text{A m}^2$.
$q_m=\dfrac{m}{2l}=\dfrac{0.2}{0.04}=5\ \text{A m}$.
solution.why_not_others: 0.2 is the moment itself, not the pole strength. 10 A m comes from dividing by l (2 cm) instead of 2l. 0.008 comes from multiplying by the length instead of dividing.
solution.common_trap: Using the half-length l in place of the magnetic length 2l.

questions.question: Given below are two statements: Assertion A and Reason R. Choose the correct answer.

statements.A: The net magnetic flux through a closed surface that encloses only the N-pole of a long bar magnet is positive.
statements.R: Magnetic field lines are continuous closed loops.

options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

solution.key_concept: Gauss's law for magnetism: $\oint\vec{B}\cdot d\vec{A}=0$ for every closed surface.
steps: Field lines form closed loops, so every line leaving a closed surface also enters it.
The net flux through any closed surface is therefore zero, even one drawn around a single pole.
A is false and R is true.
solution.final_answer: Option (4): A is false but R is true
solution.why_not_others: A is false because the flux is zero, not positive. This rules out options (1), (2) and (3).
solution.common_trap: Treating a magnetic pole like an electric charge that acts as a source of net flux.
solution.time_saving_tip: Magnetic flux through any closed surface is always zero.

questions.question: Given below are two statements. Choose the most appropriate answer.

statements.I: When a bar magnet is cut along its axis into two equal halves, the pole strength of each half stays the same and its magnetic moment is halved.
statements.II: Two magnetic field lines may intersect at a point where the fields of two different magnets superpose.

options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct

solution.key_concept: An axial cut halves both pole strength and moment. Field lines never cross.
steps: Cutting along the axis halves the pole area, so $q_m$ is halved. The length is unchanged, so $m$ is also halved. Statement I is incorrect.
The resultant field has a unique direction at every point, so lines cannot intersect. Statement II is incorrect.
solution.final_answer: Option (2): Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
solution.why_not_others: Statement I describes a perpendicular cut, not an axial cut. Statement II ignores the fact that superposed fields give a single net direction at each point.
solution.common_trap: Swapping the results of perpendicular and axial cuts.

questions.question: For a short bar magnet, the ratio of the magnitude of the field at a point on its axial line to that at a point on its equatorial line at the same distance from the centre is:

solution.key_concept: For a short magnet, $B_{ax}=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{2m}{r^3}$ and $B_{eq}=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{m}{r^3}$.
steps: Divide the two expressions at the same r.
solution.why_not_others: $1:2$ inverts the ratio. $1:1$ ignores the factor 2. $4:1$ squares the ratio.
solution.common_trap: Inverting the ratio.

questions.question: A short bar magnet has magnetic moment $0.4\ \text{A m}^2$. The magnitude of its magnetic field at a point on its axial line $10\ \text{cm}$ from its centre is: (take $\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}=10^{-7}\ \text{T m A}^{-1}$)

solution.key_concept: Axial field of a short magnet: $B=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{2m}{r^3}$.
solution.why_not_others: $4\times10^{-5}$ T uses the equatorial formula. $8\times10^{-6}$ T uses $r^2$ instead of $r^3$. $1.0\times10^{-3}$ T uses $\mu_0$ in place of $\mu_0/4\pi$.
solution.common_trap: Dropping the factor 2 in the axial formula.

questions.question: A short bar magnet produces a field of magnitude $B_0$ at a point on its equatorial line at distance r from its centre. What is the magnitude of the field at a point at the same distance r on a line making $60^\circ$ with the magnetic axis?

solution.key_concept: $B=\frac{\mu_0 m}{4\pi r^3}\sqrt{3\cos^2\theta+1}$, and $B_0=\frac{\mu_0 m}{4\pi r^3}$.
steps: $\cos60^\circ=\tfrac12$, so $3\cos^2\theta+1=\tfrac34+1=\tfrac74$.
$B=B_0\sqrt{7/4}=\dfrac{\sqrt7}{2}B_0$.
solution.why_not_others: $\frac{\sqrt{13}}{2}B_0$ uses $\cos30^\circ$, measuring the angle from the equator instead of the axis. $\frac74B_0$ forgets the square root. $\sqrt7B_0$ drops the factor $\frac12$.
solution.common_trap: Measuring $\theta$ from the equatorial line instead of the axis.
solution.time_saving_tip: Check the limits: $\theta=90^\circ$ gives $B_0$ and $\theta=0$ gives $2B_0$, so the answer must lie between them.

questions.question: Match List-I with List-II and choose the correct answer.

list_I.label: A
list_I.text: Axial field of a short magnet of moment m at distance r

list_I.label: B
list_I.text: Equatorial field of the same magnet at distance r

list_I.label: C
list_I.text: Axial field of the same magnet at distance 2r

list_I.label: D
list_I.text: Equatorial field of the same magnet at distance 2r

solution.key_concept: For a short magnet, $B_{ax}=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{2m}{r^3}$ and $B_{eq}=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{m}{r^3}$. Both vary as $1/r^3$.
steps: A: $\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{2m}{r^3}$, which is II.
B: $\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{m}{r^3}$, which is IV.
C: $\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{2m}{8r^3}=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{m}{4r^3}$, which is III.
D: $\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{m}{8r^3}$, which is I.
solution.why_not_others: Options (1) and (4) swap the axial and equatorial forms. Option (3) forgets the factor 2 at distance 2r and mismatches C and D.
solution.common_trap: Assuming the field halves or quarters when the distance doubles, instead of falling to 1/8.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about the field of a bar magnet are correct?

statements.A: For a short magnet, the field on the axial line is directed along $\vec{m}$.
statements.B: For a short magnet, the field on the equatorial line is directed along $\vec{m}$.
statements.C: Doubling the distance from a short magnet reduces its field to one-eighth.
statements.D: The exact axial expression $\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{2mr}{(r^2-l^2)^2}$ reduces to $\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{2m}{r^3}$ when $r\gg l$.
statements.E: At a fixed distance, the field of a short magnet is maximum on the equatorial line ($\theta=90^\circ$).

solution.key_concept: Axial field: along m, $\propto 2m/r^3$. Equatorial field: opposite to m, $\propto m/r^3$.
steps: A is true: the axial field points along m.
B is false: the equatorial field points opposite to m.
C is true: since $B\propto1/r^3$, doubling r gives 1/8 of the field.
D is true: for $r\gg l$, $(r^2-l^2)^2\approx r^4$, giving $\frac{2m}{r^3}$.
E is false: $\sqrt{3\cos^2\theta+1}$ is largest at $\theta=0$, on the axis.
solution.final_answer: Option (3): A, C and D only
solution.why_not_others: Option (1) misses the true statement D. Option (2) includes the false statement B. Option (4) includes the false statement E and omits A.
solution.common_trap: Assuming the equatorial field is along m, as the axial field is.

questions.question: A bar magnet of magnetic moment $2\ \text{A m}^2$ is placed in a uniform field of $0.5\ \text{T}$ with its axis at $30^\circ$ to the field. The magnitude of the torque on it is:

solution.key_concept: $\tau=mB\sin\theta$.
steps: $\tau=2\times0.5\times\sin30^\circ$.
$\tau=1\times0.5=0.5\ \text{N m}$.
solution.why_not_others: 0.87 N m uses $\cos30^\circ$. 1.0 N m omits $\sin\theta$. 0.25 N m applies the factor 0.5 twice.
solution.common_trap: Using cosine in place of sine.

questions.question: A magnetic dipole of moment $1.5\ \text{A m}^2$ is in a uniform field of $0.4\ \text{T}$. The work required to rotate it from $\theta=60^\circ$ to $\theta=180^\circ$ with respect to the field is:

solution.key_concept: $W=mB(\cos\theta_1-\cos\theta_2)$.
solution.why_not_others: 0.3 J comes from the sign error $\cos180^\circ=+1$. 1.2 J is the work from $0^\circ$ to $180^\circ$. 0.6 J is just mB, the work from $0^\circ$ to $90^\circ$.
solution.common_trap: Making a sign error with $\cos180^\circ=-1$.

questions.question: A freely suspended magnet performs small angular oscillations with a period of $3\ \text{s}$ in a uniform magnetic field. If the field is made nine times stronger, the new period is:

solution.key_concept: $T=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{I}{mB}}$, so $T\propto\frac{1}{\sqrt B}$.
steps: $T'/T=\sqrt{B/9B}=\tfrac13$.
$T'=3\times\tfrac13=1\ \text{s}$.
solution.why_not_others: 27 s assumes $T\propto B$. 9 s assumes $T\propto\sqrt B$. $\frac13$ s assumes $T\propto1/B$.
solution.common_trap: Forgetting the square root in the period formula.

questions.question: Given below are two statements: Assertion A and Reason R. Choose the correct answer.

statements.A: A bar magnet placed in a uniform magnetic field with its moment antiparallel to the field is in unstable equilibrium.
statements.R: The potential energy $U=-mB\cos\theta$ of the magnet is maximum at $\theta=180^\circ$.

options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

solution.key_concept: Equilibrium at maximum potential energy is unstable.
steps: At $\theta=180^\circ$, the torque $mB\sin\theta=0$, so the magnet is in equilibrium.
$U=+mB$ is the maximum value, so any small displacement lowers U and the magnet turns away.
R therefore explains why A is true.
solution.final_answer: Option (1): Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
solution.why_not_others: Both statements are true, so options (3) and (4) fail. The maximum potential energy in R is exactly why the equilibrium in A is unstable, so option (2) fails.
solution.common_trap: Thinking zero torque always means stable equilibrium.

questions.question: Given below are two statements. Choose the most appropriate answer.

statements.I: A bar magnet placed in a uniform magnetic field experiences a net force along the field in addition to a torque.
statements.II: In a uniform field, the work needed to rotate a magnetic dipole from $\theta=0^\circ$ to $90^\circ$ is half the work needed to rotate it from $0^\circ$ to $180^\circ$.

options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct

solution.key_concept: In a uniform field the net force is zero, and $W=mB(\cos\theta_1-\cos\theta_2)$.
steps: In a uniform field the forces on the two poles are equal and opposite, so the net force is zero. Statement I is incorrect.
$W_{0\to90}=mB$ and $W_{0\to180}=2mB$, so the first is half the second. Statement II is correct.
solution.final_answer: Option (4): Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
solution.why_not_others: A net force acts only in a non-uniform field, so Statement I is false. The ratio of works is exactly 1:2, so Statement II is true.
solution.common_trap: Assuming any magnetic field must exert a net force on a magnet.

questions.question: Which of the following substances is diamagnetic?

solution.key_concept: Diamagnetic substances have small negative susceptibility. Examples are Bi, Cu, Pb, Si, water, $N_2$ and NaCl.
steps: Bismuth is a standard diamagnetic substance.
Al and Na are paramagnetic, and Ni is ferromagnetic.
solution.why_not_others: Aluminium and sodium are paramagnetic. Nickel is ferromagnetic.
solution.common_trap: Assuming every metal is para- or ferromagnetic.

questions.question: A magnetic material placed in a magnetic intensity of $1000\ \text{A m}^{-1}$ acquires a magnetisation of $2.5\times10^{5}\ \text{A m}^{-1}$. Its relative permeability is:

solution.key_concept: $\chi=M/H$ and $\mu_r=1+\chi$.
solution.why_not_others: 250 is the susceptibility, not $\mu_r$. 249 comes from $\chi-1$. $4\times10^{-3}$ is $H/M$, the inverted ratio.
solution.common_trap: Reporting $\chi$ as $\mu_r$.

questions.question: A liquid is filled in a U-tube, and one limb is placed between the poles of a strong electromagnet. When the field is switched on, the liquid level in that limb falls. The liquid could be:

solution.key_concept: A diamagnetic liquid is depressed in the limb placed in the field, while a paramagnetic liquid rises.
steps: A falling level means the liquid moves from the stronger field to the weaker field, so it is diamagnetic.
Water is diamagnetic.
solution.why_not_others: Oxygen, $CuCl_2$ and aluminium are paramagnetic, so their level would rise in the field.
solution.common_trap: Reversing the U-tube behaviour of para- and diamagnetic liquids.

questions.question: Match List-I with List-II and choose the correct answer.

solution.key_concept: Each class of magnetic material has a characteristic susceptibility.
steps: A superconductor is a perfect diamagnet, with $\chi=-1$: I.
Copper is diamagnetic, with small negative $\chi$: II.
Aluminium is paramagnetic, with small positive $\chi$: III.
Iron is ferromagnetic, with $\chi\gg1$: IV.
solution.why_not_others: Options (2) and (4) swap the superconductor and copper. Option (3) swaps copper and aluminium. Option (4) also swaps aluminium and iron.
solution.common_trap: Treating copper as paramagnetic.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about magnetic materials are correct?

statements.A: Diamagnetism is present in all materials but is masked when para- or ferromagnetism exists.
statements.B: For a diamagnetic substance, the relative permeability is slightly greater than 1.
statements.C: The fields are related by $B=\mu_0(H+M)$, and $\mu_r=1+\chi$.
statements.D: A paramagnetic rod suspended freely in a uniform field aligns perpendicular to the field.
statements.E: Diamagnetic susceptibility does not depend on temperature.

solution.key_concept: Properties of dia-, para- and ferromagnetic materials and the relations among B, H, M and $\chi$.
steps: A is true, as stated in the properties of diamagnetism.
B is false: for a diamagnet, $\mu_r<1$.
C is true: these are the standard relations.
D is false: a paramagnetic rod aligns parallel to the field, and a diamagnetic rod aligns perpendicular.
E is true: only paramagnets follow Curie's law, and diamagnetic $\chi$ is temperature-independent.
solution.final_answer: Option (4): A, C and E only
solution.why_not_others: Option (1) misses the true statement E. Option (2) includes the false statement B. Option (3) includes the false statements B and D.
solution.common_trap: Swapping the alignment of para- and diamagnetic rods.
